passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Catering Order That Went Wrong

emails.subject: Order 7742 — retirement lunch, 14 March
emails.body:
Dear Fernwood Catering,

I booked catering for a retirement lunch for 60 people on 14 March, order 7742, at $1,140. I want to set out what happened, because I think two separate things went wrong and only one of them is a complaint.

The food arrived 50 minutes late. That is the smaller issue: the speeches were moved and nobody went hungry.

The larger issue is that I ordered 12 vegetarian portions and 4 gluten-free portions, confirmed in writing on 2 March. Twelve vegetarian meals arrived. The gluten-free meals did not, and there was no label on anything. A guest with coeliac disease could not eat, and your driver told her the sandwiches were "probably fine". That is not a judgement a driver should be making on someone else's behalf.

I am not asking for the whole order to be refunded. The food was good and most of it was correct. I would like the gluten-free portions refunded, and I would like to know what you are changing about labelling, because the money matters far less than the second part.

Sincerely,
Dilnaz Askarova

emails.subject: RE: Order 7742 — retirement lunch, 14 March
emails.body:
Dear Ms Askarova,

Thank you for separating those two things, because you are right that they are different and the second is the serious one.

On the lateness: a road closure we had not checked. Our fault, not the city's, and we have refunded the delivery charge of $45 without you asking for it.

On the gluten-free portions. Your order was correct in our system. The kitchen made the four meals. They were left behind at the depot because they travel in a separate sealed container and the loading checklist has one line for "special dietary" rather than a count. One line cannot tell a driver whether the container is missing. The four portions are refunded at $19 each, $76, so $121 in total with the delivery charge.

On the driver. He should have said "I cannot confirm that" and phoned us. He has been told, and I would rather tell you plainly that he was wrong than explain why he thought it was reasonable.

What is changing, from Monday: the loading sheet now lists each dietary portion individually and the driver signs for the count, not the container. Allergen labels are printed with the order rather than applied in the kitchen, so an unlabelled item cannot leave. And any query about an allergen goes to the kitchen by phone — no driver answers it.

We cater about forty events a month and this has not happened before, which is not a defence. It happened once and once is the number that matters with coeliac disease.

Regards,
Marcus Ibitoye
Operations Manager

passages.title: What Food Labels Do and Do Not Tell You
passages.content:
Food labelling is often described as a transparency measure, which is only partly what it is. Most of what appears on a package is there because a regulation requires it, and the regulations were written to answer particular questions — not to give a general account of what the food is.

The clearest example is the ingredients list, which is ordered by weight at the point of manufacture. That ordering is genuinely informative and is routinely misread. A product listing flour first contains more flour than anything else by weight, but nothing follows about how much sugar it contains in total, because sugar can appear under several names at several positions. Glucose syrup, invert sugar, fruit juice concentrate and dextrose are separate entries, each individually smaller than the flour, while adding up to a larger quantity than any single ingredient.

Allergen labelling works differently and is stronger. Major allergens must be declared wherever they appear, usually emphasised in the text, and this is a legal requirement rather than a courtesy. The weakness is elsewhere: precautionary statements such as "may contain" are, in most jurisdictions, voluntary and unstandardised. A manufacturer who applies them cautiously and one who does not may produce identically risky products with different labels, and a consumer cannot distinguish the two.

Front-of-pack nutrition claims are the most regulated and the least useful. A claim like "reduced fat" is defined relative to a comparable product rather than in absolute terms, so a reduced-fat product can contain more fat than an unlabelled competitor. "No added sugar" restricts what the manufacturer put in and says nothing about what was already there. Both claims are accurate and both mislead readers who take them as statements about the food rather than about the process.

Dates are the area where consumer behaviour and regulation diverge most sharply. A use-by date is a safety instruction. A best-before date is a quality estimate set by the manufacturer, and food is frequently edible well past it. Substantial quantities of household food waste are attributed to the two being treated as equivalent, and the labels look similar by design rather than by accident, since both are printed to the same specification.

The reasonable conclusion is not that labels are dishonest. It is that each element answers one narrow question, and reading a label as a summary of the food asks it to do something it was never constructed to do.

passages.title: Should School Meals Be Free for Every Student?

viewpoints.name: Trustee Fernanda Quiroz
viewpoints.text: We ran means-tested meals for nine years and I would not go back. The saving was real and smaller than expected, because assessing eligibility, chasing forms and managing arrears costs money that never appears in the meal budget. What removed the stigma was not generosity, it was making the queue identical for everyone. I will not claim it lifted test scores; I have seen those studies and they are weaker than people quote. I claim it ended a daily sorting of children by household income, which was reason enough.

viewpoints.name: Aleksander Novotny, school business manager
viewpoints.text: I am the person who has to fund this and my objection is not the meals. It is that universal programmes are announced with capital money and no operating line. My kitchen was built for 300 covers and serves 700; the constraint is serving time, dishwashing capacity and staff, not food cost. Fund the meals without funding the kitchen and you get a two-hour lunch rotation that eats teaching time. I would rather have a funded programme for half the school than an unfunded one for all of it.

viewpoints.name: Dr Priyasha Raman, public health researcher
viewpoints.text: The evidence for universal provision is good on participation and weak on the outcomes campaigners lead with. Take-up rises sharply when meals are free for all — that is consistent and well measured. The attainment and obesity findings are noisier, often short-term, and rarely control for what the meal replaced. I support the policy, and I want it argued for on the ground where the evidence is strong, because overstating it now invites the whole thing to be dismissed when a better-designed study lands.

viewpoints.name: Owen Baptiste, catering supervisor
viewpoints.text: Everyone debating this should look at what gets thrown away. Universal free meals do increase waste in the first year, and the reason is not fussiness — it is menus designed for the children who used to pay, served to children who never chose them. The schools that fixed it did the same thing: they asked the students what they would actually eat and changed the menu. Nobody funds that consultation because it is not capital and it is not food, and it is the cheapest part of the whole programme.
